claims.text: Zirconium-alloy nuclear-fuel cladding is susceptible to rapid high-temperature steam oxidation during accident scenarios.
Introducing aluminum into a CrN coating by PVD will produce a CrAlN ceramic coating on zirconium-alloy cladding.
A moderate PVD deposition temperature of approximately 400°C can incorporate a controlled amount of aluminum into the CrN matrix.
CrAlN exposed to steam at approximately 1200°C will form a continuous, dense alpha-Al2O3 surface layer.
The continuous, dense alpha-Al2O3 layer will act as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
At high temperature, aluminum incorporated in CrAlN preferentially oxidizes to alumina.
The resulting alumina scale will be stable and adherent.
The alumina scale will minimize oxygen ingress and reduce oxidation kinetics.
The underlying CrN structure will maintain mechanical stability at high temperature.
The underlying CrN structure will minimize alterations to neutron interactions.
CrAlN-coated cladding will have a statistically significant reduction in oxidation weight gain relative to uncoated zirconium-alloy cladding.
CrAlN-coated cladding will have a statistically significant reduction in oxidation weight gain relative to standard CrN-coated cladding.
CrAlN-coated cladding will exhibit improved oxide-scale integrity relative to both uncoated and standard CrN-coated cladding.
The CrAlN coating will retain service integrity on zirconium-alloy cladding.
The intervention will remain effective under transient high-temperature steam oxidation conditions up to approximately 1200°C.
The intervention will remain effective under steady high-temperature steam oxidation conditions up to approximately 1200°C.
Effectiveness depends on the PVD process producing a uniform and adherent coating.
Steam exposure at approximately 1200°C simulates both routine and accident conditions.
